description: A single-panel error-bar plot of slip band spacing versus engineering strain for three hot-rolling reductions. The y-axis is labelled "Slip band spacing (nm)" and runs 0-350 nm with gridlines every 50 nm; the x-axis is labelled "Engineering strain" and runs 0.0-0.5 with ticks every 0.1, with data points plotted at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4. The legend lists three samples: HR45 (grey filled squares), HR68 (red open circles) and HR82 (blue open triangles); every marker carries a vertical error bar. At engineering strain 0.1 the three samples are strongly separated — the HR45 marker sits essentially on the 300 nm gridline, HR68 lies between the 150 and 200 nm gridlines, and HR82 sits just above the 50 nm gridline — with the largest error bars on HR45 (spanning roughly 250-350 nm) and the smallest on HR82. By strain 0.2 the HR45 curve has fallen steeply to just above the 100 nm gridline while HR68 and HR82 have dropped close to the 50 nm gridline; from 0.2 to 0.4 the curves flatten and converge at approximately 50 nm. The panel therefore shows that slip band spacing refines continuously with plastic strain, that refinement is faster and saturates earlier for the larger hot-rolling reductions, and that all three samples converge to a common lower-bound spacing.

subfigures.description: Error-bar line plot of slip band spacing (nm, y-axis, 0-350) versus engineering strain (x-axis, 0.0-0.5) with data at strains 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4 for the HR45 (grey squares), HR68 (red circles) and HR82 (blue triangles) samples; all curves fall steeply to a plateau at about 50 nm.

observations.observation: The axes are labelled "Slip band spacing (nm)" (y, 0-350 nm, gridlines every 50 nm) and "Engineering strain" (x, 0.0-0.5, ticks every 0.1), so the figure reports a microstructural length scale against imposed plastic strain.
The legend contains exactly three entries: HR45 (grey filled squares), HR68 (red open circles) and HR82 (blue open triangles).
Markers are plotted at only three engineering strains, 0.1, 0.2 and 0.4, with no data point at 0.3 or 0.5.

At engineering strain 0.1 the HR45 marker lies essentially on the 300 nm gridline, HR68 between the 150 and 200 nm gridlines, and HR82 just above the 50 nm gridline; each carries a vertical error bar, largest for HR45 (spanning roughly 250-350 nm) and smallest for HR82.
At engineering strain 0.2 all three curves have dropped sharply: HR45 sits just above the 100 nm gridline, while HR68 and HR82 fall close to the 50 nm gridline.
At engineering strain 0.4 the three curves converge on approximately the 50 nm gridline, showing that slip band spacing stops decreasing once it reaches this level.
Ranking is identical at every plotted strain: HR45 > HR68 > HR82 in slip band spacing, i.e. the larger the hot-rolling reduction the smaller the spacing at a given strain.
The caption states the figure shows the evolution of slip band spacing as a function of engineering strain of the investigated samples at different hot-rolling reductions.

The citing text quantifies the spacings at engineering strain 0.1 as 296.40 ± 50.06 nm (HR45), 155.02 ± 38.42 nm (HR68) and 68.05 ± 8.91 nm (HR82), values that match the marker positions read from the plot.

The citing text states that the slip band spacing barely changed after reducing to ~50 nm, indicating that slip band refinement during stage II was saturated and could provide no additional strain-hardening effect.

The citing text states that the deformation substructure evolved faster in samples with larger hot-rolling reductions, attributing this to finer initial grain size and the resulting earlier termination of individual slip bands.

The citing text states that the faster slip band refinement in the finer-grained (higher-reduction) samples caused earlier saturation, earlier microband formation and a shorter stage II, explaining the slight ductility loss.

unreadable_items: Exact error-bar extents at engineering strains 0.2 and 0.4 are too small to read precisely (bars overlap the markers); only the 0.1 error bars are large enough to gauge approximately.
